overview: I study decisions that are linked by shared resources, material flows and commitments over time. Production plans determine what can be shipped. Operating-room schedules affect demand for ward beds. A decision to restore one facility may have little effect until a supplier or transport link is available. Across these settings, I ask which decisions need to be made jointly and what is lost when they are made independently.

My methodological work combines mathematical programming, decomposition and adaptive search. Formulations identify the constraints that couple decisions. Decomposition exploits parts of the problem that can be solved separately, while learning can direct search toward more promising changes to a plan. My published work tests these ideas in freight and maritime operations. My current and prospective work extends them to automated systems, healthcare and disruption response.

algorithms.question: How can mathematical structure, learning and emerging computational methods improve modeling, algorithms and sequential decisions?
paragraphs: My methodological interests concern how decision problems should be represented and solved. Assignment, sequencing, timing, energy and resource availability impose different structures, with consequences for formulation and decomposition. I am interested in identifying which decisions must be coordinated, which subproblems admit efficient solution, and how useful bounds and structural properties can guide computation.

My published work develops compact mixed-integer formulations, decomposition approaches and adaptive hyperheuristics. Berth scheduling and cross-docking provide settings in which modeling and algorithmic choices can be examined together. Related questions concern how exact optimization should be combined with approximate search, and how computational effort should be allocated as a solution evolves.

I am interested in learning-informed decisions under changing information. Reinforcement learning can connect current choices with future resource availability and observations. Generative AI raises questions about representing operating requirements, constructing formulations and revising models through mathematical checks and solver feedback. Agentic systems introduce a further question: how should information and decision authority be shared when several planners control interdependent activities?

Developing quantum-assisted routing research examines feasible sampling for routes with time windows through ordered mixing and branch allocation. My broader interest is how emerging computational methods can be integrated with classical optimization. Comparisons should establish their contribution to feasibility, solution quality and scalability within the complete method.
questions: Which dependencies must be represented explicitly, and which admit decomposition without losing feasibility or useful bounds?
How should computation be allocated between adaptive exploration and exact improvement?
Under what conditions do learned strategies transfer across problem instances, and how should solver feedback guide AI-generated models and algorithms?
algorithms.lead: I develop formulations and algorithms for optimization problems with coupled assignments, sequences and schedules. My work examines when a compact formulation can make exact optimization tractable, when to decompose a problem, and how to allocate computation between exploring alternatives and improving a promising solution.

focus.title: Mathematical representation
focus.text: Compact formulations can remove redundant decisions while preserving the relationships that determine whether an operating plan is feasible.

focus.title: Decomposition and adaptive computation

focus.title: Learning within decision processes
focus.text: I am investigating whether operating data can guide decisions under uncertainty and whether AI-assisted formulations preserve the constraints intended by the modeler. In both cases, the test is the feasibility and quality of the resulting decisions.

focus.title: Emerging computational methods
focus.text: Quantum-assisted routing examines feasible sampling with time windows. I am interested in the contribution of quantum and classical components to one complete method.

maritime.question: How should decisions within operating systems and across organizations be coordinated, and how does that coordination affect performance and incentives?
paragraphs: My interests in operations and supply chains span sourcing, production, inventory, distribution and service delivery. These decisions interact through material requirements, capacity, timing and information. I am interested in when joint planning creates value, when participants can retain local authority, and how contracts or shared-capacity arrangements sustain coordination under uncertainty.

At container terminals, vessel arrival times, berth availability and service order determine when ships can be handled. My research develops compact mixed-integer formulations and adaptive search methods for assigning berths and sequencing service. In liner shipping, I study how schedule recovery decisions balance service commitments, operating costs and emissions. At cross-docks, the corresponding coordination problem is to align inbound and outbound truck schedules with the freight transfers between them.

My longer-term interests extend from facility scheduling to coordination across firms. Production sequences change material requirements and delivery timing; shipment consolidation can reduce transport costs while delaying inputs needed downstream. I plan to investigate these dependencies through integrated sourcing, inventory, production and distribution models. Related questions concern information sharing, capacity agreements and the distribution of coordination gains when participating organizations have different objectives.

Industrial and automated systems introduce additional dependencies among equipment, transport, processing and reusable resources. My developing quay-crane and laboratory scheduling work examines when resources become available for subsequent tasks. Longer-term questions concern integrated production and material handling, the location of bottlenecks, and how automation changes the relationship between capacity and scheduling.

Product characteristics can change the coordination problem as much as facility capacity. My collaborative pharmaceutical-supply-chain review separates medicine distribution from reverse collection, sorting, recovery, recycling and disposal. Its content analysis and conceptual framework connect planning decisions with cold-chain requirements, resilience and sustainability. This work motivates broader interests in coordinating material flows across an entire product lifecycle, including systems with perishability and limited recovery options.

Maritime decarbonization links investment commitments with the conditions required for operating use. My shore-power study develops an implementation-accountability framework and applies it to the Northwest Seaport Alliance and Seattle cruise operations. The analysis distinguishes infrastructure commitments, project readiness, activity coverage and actual vessel connection. Together with work on electric tugboats, it motivates questions about complementary investments, utilization and the operating consequences of technology adoption.
questions: How do upstream and downstream dependencies change bottlenecks and the value of processing, storage or transport capacity?
How do information sharing, contractual commitments and decision authority affect coordination and the distribution of benefits?
How should technology adoption and supporting infrastructure be planned alongside the operating policies that determine their value?
maritime.lead: I study how decisions made by producers, carriers, terminal operators and service providers affect one another. Port and freight operations offer concrete examples: an assignment at one stage changes the timing and capacity available at the next. The same coordination problem arises when firms plan production, inventory and distribution separately.

focus.title: Automation and resource circulation

focus.title: Product lifecycles and investment
focus.text: My work on pharmaceutical supply chains considers product returns and recovery. My work on shore power examines how infrastructure commitments translate into implementation responsibilities and actual use.

resilience.question: How should systems invest in flexibility and adapt operating commitments when disruption changes what is feasible?
paragraphs: My interests in resilience connect advance system design with adaptation during operations. Inventory, alternative suppliers, reserve equipment, access routes and supporting energy resources create different recovery options. Their value depends on the activities they enable and the dependencies they leave unresolved. I plan to study preparedness and restoration across supply chains, industrial systems and essential services.

Electrification connects investment choices with daily schedules. My collaborative review of electric-vehicle scheduling distinguishes general operating constraints from power-grid and environmental considerations, with representative models for each category. Related electric-tugboat research combines literature analysis, industry interviews and economic assessment. Together, these studies motivate questions about charging capacity, utilization and financing that cannot be answered from equipment specifications alone.

Healthcare operations connect scheduling with patient flow, service urgency and resources occupied over time. My developing surgery-and-ward research links operating-room and surgeon availability with downstream bed occupancy. Broader interests include coordinating service capacity, staffing and schedules under uncertain demand and duration, and understanding how local decisions affect access and continuity elsewhere in a service system.

Humanitarian and emergency operations introduce changing needs, disrupted access and competing service priorities. My sponsored-project experience includes strategic humanitarian logistics, while developing flood-response research examines task scheduling and resource allocation. Longer-term questions concern preparedness, distributed response and recovery when information, transport access or replenishment is intermittent.
questions: How should reserve capacity, inventory and alternative resources be positioned when their value depends on the recovery policy?
Which commitments should be protected or revised as disruption information changes?
How can allocation models evaluate service and access together with energy, environmental and economic consequences?
resilience.lead: I study how decisions made before a disruption shape the options available during recovery. Reserve capacity, alternative suppliers and flexible schedules protect different parts of a system. Their value depends on which services can continue, which resources can be reassigned, and in what order disrupted operations can resume.

focus.title: Preparedness and recovery
focus.text: Alternative supply, inventory, reserve equipment and access routes protect different activities. Their value depends on restoration order and dependencies elsewhere in a network.

focus.title: Electrification and automation
focus.text: I examine how electrification and automation affect schedules, equipment utilization and service. An investment may relieve one constraint while increasing demand for charging, maintenance or handling capacity elsewhere.

focus.title: Healthcare and laboratory services
focus.text: Developing research connects surgery schedules with ward occupancy and laboratory schedules with resource release and reuse. Broader questions concern capacity, uncertainty and service continuity.

focus.title: Humanitarian and emergency operations
focus.text: Sponsored humanitarian-logistics work and developing flood-response studies examine scarce resources, changing needs and access constraints. My long-term interests connect preparedness with distributed response and recovery.

futureNotes.question: How should reserve capacity, inventory and alternative resources be positioned when their value depends on the recovery policy?
futureNotes.text: Preparedness alternatives should be compared through the recovery actions they enable, including shared exposure and dependencies between resources.

futureNotes.question: Which commitments should be protected or revised as disruption information changes?
futureNotes.text: Replanning can preserve valuable commitments or retain an unsuitable plan. The research question is when local revision is sufficient and when coordination is required.

futureNotes.question: How can allocation models evaluate service and access together with energy, environmental and economic consequences?
futureNotes.text: Service delay, unmet need and geographic access can change differently. Models should make these consequences visible alongside cost and environmental performance.

cases.title: Compact formulations and decomposition for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A compact berth-scheduling formulation supports Benders decomposition and column generation for larger planning problems.
cases.question: How does formulation design affect the scalability of exact berth-scheduling optimization?
cases.approach: The study minimizes total vessel service costs in dynamic, discrete berth scheduling. Two-dimensional decision variables, the removal of redundant model elements and simplified sequencing reduce the size of the mixed-integer formulation. Benders decomposition and column generation exploit the resulting structure to address larger scheduling instances.
cases.evidence: The computational study compares the formulation with five mathematical models and three metaheuristics. It reports solutions for instances with more than 260 vessels within two hours under the tested settings, alongside sensitivity analysis of operational parameters.
cases.meaning: The formulation removes redundant sequencing variables and constraints while retaining the decisions that determine a feasible berth schedule. That representation also provides a basis for Benders decomposition and column generation.
cases.connection: The formulation and decomposition ideas may also apply to problems that combine resource assignments with sequencing.
cases.futureQuestion: How can compact formulations be extended to coordinated resource decisions when berthing, handling and downstream service interact?

figure.caption: Marine container terminal operations, reproduced from Figure 1 of the berth-scheduling study.

cases.title: Integrated truck scheduling and freight-transfer coordination
cases.summary: A mixed-integer model, precedence-consistent batching and pricing-guided search coordinate truck services with freight transfers and shared handling capacity.
cases.question: How should freight transfers, handling capacity and service precedence be represented in integrated truck schedules?
cases.approach: The mixed-integer model coordinates dock assignments, service sequences and timing across inbound unloading, freight transfer and outbound loading. It accounts for waiting, handling, temporary storage and departure-delay costs. Sequential fix-and-optimize constructs precedence-consistent batches. Pricing-guided search uses reduced-cost information to identify promising single-truck reinsertions, with exact evaluation after discrete scheduling decisions are fixed.
cases.evidence: The experiments compare the formulation with two established models and evaluate both solution frameworks. On large tested instances, reported objective improvements reach approximately 30% relative to the comparison methods. Pricing-guided search reduces mean runtime by more than 35% relative to solving the proposed model directly.
cases.meaning: The two methods exploit freight-transfer precedence in different ways. Sequential fix-and-optimize builds schedules in batches consistent with freight availability. Pricing-guided search uses cost information to select promising changes to truck assignments and sequences.
cases.connection: This work motivates my interest in coordinating schedules across processing, transfer and service stages.
cases.futureQuestion: When should additional processing or storage capacity be preferred to improved coordination of inbound and outbound operations?

figure.caption: Inbound unloading, internal handling and outbound loading at a cross-docking terminal; Figure 1 of the study.

cases.title: Thompson Sampling for adaptive scheduling heuristics
cases.summary: Thompson Sampling adapts operator selection while repair and exact evaluation address schedule feasibility and accuracy.
cases.question: How can adaptive operator selection improve search while preserving reliable schedule evaluation?
cases.approach: The Hybridized Thompson Sampling Hyperheuristic combines evolutionary search with an adaptive operator-selection controller. A repair-and-penalty mechanism handles inbound–outbound precedence constraints. Fast approximate fitness evaluation supports exploration, while exact optimization refines schedule evaluation.
cases.evidence: On the reported benchmark instances, the algorithm produces solutions comparable with exact optimization for small problems and improves on the comparison metaheuristics. The paper reports improvements of up to approximately 24% and an average runtime of 186.71 seconds across its experimental setting.
cases.meaning: Thompson Sampling uses observed improvements to choose among search operators. Repair and penalties address precedence violations, while approximate evaluation keeps exploration inexpensive. Exact service-time optimization refines the evaluation of promising schedules.
cases.connection: A next question is whether the learned search strategies remain useful under different demand patterns and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: Can adaptive search strategies transfer between demand patterns and facilities while preserving feasible schedules?

figure.caption: The study’s hyperheuristic workflow, including operator selection, constraint repair and approximate or exact evaluation.

cases.title: Hybrid hyperheuristics and exact optimization for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A berth-scheduling hyperheuristic adapts genetic operators and periodically applies problem-specific exact improvement.
cases.question: How can adaptive search and exact subproblem optimization complement one another in berth scheduling?
cases.approach: The Hyperheuristic Hybridized with Exact Optimization addresses dynamic, discrete berth allocation and scheduling. It chooses genetic operators according to their observed performance and periodically applies berth-specific exact optimization procedures to improve candidate schedules.
cases.evidence: Computational comparisons examine the algorithm against exact-optimization-inspired methods and established metaheuristics. Component experiments investigate the contribution of hyperheuristic control and hybridization. Scenario analysis considers berth availability, vessel arrival intensity and departure-delay penalties.
cases.meaning: The algorithm allocates computation between exploration across genetic operators and exact improvement of berth-specific schedules. Operator performance changes during search, so the controller uses observed results to revise its choices. Component experiments examine what is gained from adaptation and exact improvement within the combined procedure.
cases.connection: I am interested in how to divide computation between broad search and exact improvement in other scheduling problems.
cases.futureQuestion: How should limited computation be divided between broad search and structured exact improvement as a planning problem changes?

figure.caption: A marine container terminal, illustrating the berth and handling resources linked by a schedule.

cases.title: Optimization for highway–rail crossing closure decisions
cases.summary: An optimization framework considers safety, economic and environmental effects alongside delay and maintenance costs.
cases.question: How should safety, economic and environmental effects enter the prioritization of rail-crossing closures?
cases.approach: The study develops an optimization model that includes safety, economic and environmental benefits as well as traffic-delay and maintenance implications. A sorting-inspired heuristic addresses the resulting decision problem. Computational experiments use crossings in Florida.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use Florida crossing data to compare the sorting-inspired heuristic with an exact method. Across the reported instances, it was approximately twenty times faster, with an average optimality gap of 0.14%. Sensitivity analyses examine how model inputs affect the selected closures.
cases.meaning: Related collaborative research extends closure selection to the allocation of crossing interventions. The 2026 study compares countermeasure installation, grade separation and closure under budget and feasibility constraints. Experiments with 5,939 publicly managed Florida crossings examine safety and socio-environmental trade-offs, including delay, emissions, noise and community disruption. Together, these studies distinguish selecting an intervention from evaluating the consequences of an intervention portfolio.
cases.connection: My interest is in infrastructure investment models that make competing consequences explicit. The related multi-objective study is listed in the publication record under DOI 10.1016/j.scs.2026.107485.
cases.futureQuestion: How can infrastructure prioritization represent uncertainty and changes in access, exposure and operating conditions?

cases.title: Ship schedule recovery under environmental policies
cases.summary: Multi-objective optimization examines the tension between schedule recovery, monetary losses and speed-reduction incentives.
cases.question: How should disruption recovery be planned when service targets conflict with environmental requirements and incentives?
cases.approach: The model balances monetary losses and port-arrival delays while representing emission-control areas and voluntary speed-reduction incentives. These policies affect the recovery options directly: faster sailing may recover time, while reduced speed can earn an incentive. Dynamic secant approximation and an epsilon-constraint method generate alternative recovery plans.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use the South East Asia Pendulum shipping route, with sensitivity analysis exploring how different settings affect recovery choices.
cases.meaning: The study makes the conflict between recovering service and complying with environmental restrictions explicit. A separate 2023 Computers & Industrial Engineering paper develops exact Pareto optimization for late arrivals and profit loss, including speed adjustment and port skipping. The two studies examine related recovery decisions through different models and solution methods.
cases.connection: My broader interest is in recovery policies that recognize both the value and the cost of changing commitments. The two ship-recovery papers provide examples of how operational and policy constraints alter the alternatives available after disruption.
cases.futureQuestion: Which commitments should be preserved during recovery, and where does flexibility provide the greatest value before a disruption?

approach: My teaching aims to develop analytical understanding, independent judgment and the ability to communicate a defensible recommendation. Students should learn to formulate a question, identify relevant evidence, choose an appropriate method and assess what the result supports. This approach connects mathematical modeling and computation with engineering and managerial decisions.

I build from worked examples and guided practice toward open-ended analysis. My graduate teaching experience includes optimization methods, scheduling, resource allocation and freight operations. Broader teaching interests include operations research, analytics, production and service scheduling, logistics and supply chain management. Python and R can connect these subjects through modeling, data analysis and computational implementation.

I am interested in teaching the relationship between descriptive evidence, prediction and decisions. A more accurate prediction may have little operating value when capacity or prior commitments prevent a response. Projects can ask students to compare alternatives under changing assumptions and explain the consequences. Generative AI can support exploration, with students responsible for checking evidence, calculations and their own conclusions.

Staged project proposals, preliminary analyses and revisions provide opportunities for feedback as students develop independence. Different levels of mathematical and programming preparation call for clear expectations, targeted practice and opportunities for consultation. My instructional plans emphasize individual reasoning alongside collaborative work, including interpretation, sensitivity analysis and communication to technical and managerial audiences.
teaching.mentoring: I have guided undergraduate and master’s researchers at Florida State University and currently support master’s research at the University of North Florida, where I serve as an external master’s thesis committee member. My approach connects question development, study design, analytical methods, interpretation and scholarly writing. As projects progress, students assume greater responsibility for technical decisions and develop questions of their own. My longer-term mentoring goals include sustained undergraduate investigations, graduate research and opportunities for presentations and coauthored publications.

principles.text: Students check whether a solution satisfies the operating constraints and examine which assumptions would change their recommendation.

principles.text: Worked examples lead to guided practice, project proposals and revisions, with increasing responsibility for methods and communication.

community: I have participated in prospective-student outreach and supported students preparing research showcases and competitions.
I present research at operations research and transportation conferences and review manuscripts in optimization, logistics and transportation.

agenda.title: Learning and optimization
agenda.question: When does better information change a decision?
agenda.text: I plan to connect learned information with resource constraints and prior commitments. Generative models could help formulate operating requirements; solver feedback would guide revision. Coordinated agents raise related questions about shared information, decision authority and human intervention.

agenda.title: Coordination across organizations
agenda.question: Which decisions need to be made together?
agenda.text: Production, inventory and distribution may be controlled by participants with different objectives. I am interested in which dependencies require joint planning, when local authority can be retained, and how agreements distribute coordination benefits and risks.

agenda.title: Preparedness and recovery
agenda.question: Which resources create useful recovery options?
agenda.text: Inventory, alternative supply, backup energy and reserve equipment protect service through different dependencies. I plan to examine restoration order and resource reassignment, including cases where a recovered facility cannot operate until another connection is restored.

agenda.title: Technology and sustainable operations
agenda.question: When should complementary investments enter service together?
agenda.text: Automation and electrification can relocate bottlenecks. Research would connect equipment and supporting infrastructure with operating schedules, maintenance and energy requirements, comparing phased adoption through utilization, service, lifecycle cost and emissions.

agenda.title: Healthcare and essential services
agenda.question: How do local schedules affect downstream access and continuity?
agenda.text: Surgery schedules occupy ward capacity; laboratory tasks delay reusable resources; emergency deliveries depend on changing access. These settings motivate connected models of capacity, allocation and adaptation, evaluated through delays, unmet needs and continuity of service.

currentWork.title: AI for transportation infrastructure inventories
currentWork.text: In 2026, I helped develop proposals on infrastructure inventories, speed management and sidewalk condition assessment. The inventory and assessment proposals draw on computer vision and geospatial data, with field validation where proposed. My proposed roles are co-principal investigator on the speed-management inventory and rural-to-town corridor studies and research assistant on the active-transportation inventory and sidewalk-assessment studies.

currentWork.title: Integrated scheduling and resource circulation
currentWork.text: Current investigations address automated quay-crane scheduling and laboratory scheduling with resource-release and reuse requirements. Processing completion does not always release a resource: equipment may still need to be transported, returned or prepared for its next operation. The research examines formulations and solution methods that preserve these dependencies while coordinating schedules and shared capacity.

currentWork.title: Planning under time and capacity constraints
currentWork.text: Developing studies examine flood-emergency resource allocation and joint surgery and ward scheduling. Flood-response models address task priorities and resource availability as conditions change. Healthcare scheduling connects operating-room and surgeon decisions with downstream bed occupancy. Both settings motivate questions about when to reoptimize, which commitments to retain, and how to obtain feasible plans within limited decision time.

currentWork.title: Infrastructure investment and realized use
currentWork.text: The published shore-power study develops an implementation-accountability framework for the Northwest Seaport Alliance, with Seattle cruise operations as a comparison. It distinguishes installed capability from realized connection and examines how deferral changes the activities covered by implementation plans. This work informs my broader interest in linking infrastructure investment to utilization and operating performance.

currentWork.title: Language models and operational knowledge
currentWork.text: A local research prototype retrieves passages from public transportation-agency manuals and links generated responses to source material. The research concerns the interpretation of technical requirements and the reliability of cited evidence. It also motivates a broader question: how retrieved operating rules could inform a mathematical formulation and be checked against solver feedback. The prototype remains an experimental analytical tool.

currentWork.title: Quantum-assisted optimization for constrained routing
currentWork.text: This study investigates routing with time windows through feasibility-preserving ordered mixing and branch allocation. The broader methodological question concerns how quantum sampling and classical optimization can contribute to one solution procedure. Computational comparisons examine feasibility, solution quality and scalability within the complete solution procedure.

evaluation.title: Mathematical structure and feasibility
evaluation.text: A model must represent the resource, timing and precedence relationships that determine whether a plan can be carried out. I am interested in compact formulations and decompositions that reduce computational effort while retaining these relationships.

evaluation.title: Computational comparisons
evaluation.text: Algorithms need to be compared under stated computational budgets and operating conditions. Solution quality, feasibility, time to a usable plan and sensitivity to problem size provide complementary evidence; a single best objective does not describe every planning requirement.

evaluation.title: Operating consequences
evaluation.text: The purpose of a computational result is to clarify a decision. Relevant questions include how a plan changes service, resource utilization, energy use or exposure to disruption, and which assumptions determine those effects.

contributions.title: Compact models and decomposition
contributions.text: Removing redundant sequencing decisions and exploiting assignment–timing structure can change the scale of a scheduling model.

contributions.title: Adaptive search with exact evaluation
contributions.text: Learning selects search operators; feasibility repair and exact service-time optimization address different parts of schedule quality.

contributions.title: Coordinating linked operating stages
contributions.text: Truck assignments, freight availability and shared handling capacity must remain consistent as a terminal schedule changes.
